entities.name: Augustine of Hippo
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Augustine of Hippo (born Aurelius Augustinus in Thagaste, Numidia, on November 13, 354 CE; died August 28, 430 CE, Hippo Regius) stands as the most influential Latin Church Father and a pivotal intellectual figure whose philosophical and theological works profoundly shaped Western Christianity and Western thought. Operating during the twilight of the Western Roman Empire, his writings synthesized classical philosophy with Christian doctrine, providing intellectual bedrock for medieval scholasticism and Reformation theology alike. His life spanned a period of immense upheaval, witnessing the Visigothic Sack of Rome in 410 CE, an event that directly influenced his monumental work, *The City of God*.

Following a youth marked by intellectual curiosity and hedonism, detailed in his *Confessions*, Augustine converted to Christianity in 386 CE in Milan under the influence of Bishop Ambrose. He returned to North Africa, established a monastic community, and was reluctantly ordained a priest in 391 CE, quickly rising to become Bishop of Hippo Regius in 395 CE, a position he held until his death. His episcopacy was characterized by prolific writing and vigorous theological debate, notably against the Manichaeans, Donatists, and Pelagians, articulating doctrines of original sin, divine grace, and predestination that became central to Western theology.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Augustine of Hippo profoundly shaped the intellectual and theological trajectory of Western Christianity, influencing virtually every major Christian thinker and movement for over 1500 years. His works laid the philosophical and theological foundations for the Middle Ages and the Reformation, with an impact comparable to that of Aristotle or Plato on classical thought.
